My problem is that the parent root is a Ubuntu 10.10 system. I have built a Gentoo chroot and I am invoking the fakechroot which is built and installed inside the gentoo chroot.

The fakechroot inside the Gentoo chroot is 2.15 and the glibc is 2.13. Ubuntu 10.10 is using glibc 2.12.1 I think.

I am invoking it like this:

/dvabuild/1.2/user/usr/bin/fakechroot chroot /dvabuild/1.2/user/ /bin/bash

Since fakeroot is a wrapper which uses /usr/lib64/fakechroot/libfakechroot.so, I put the gentoo .so there in the parent rootfs as well.

Using '-s' argument doesn't make a difference.

I think you are not able to reproduce because your parent root and the child chroot are congruent systems. One way to reproduce would be to 'mv /usr/bin/env /bin/env && ln -s /bin/env /usr/bin/env' inside the chroot, and making sure that /bin/env doesn't exist in the parent. Then, try running the '/usr/bin/env python' inside the chroot.

ok. You are not able to reproduce because you are mv'ing and linking after the fact, INSIDE the chroot. Any existing absolute symlinks inside the chroot are not followed by fakechroot.

What I meant was chroot (instead of fakechroot), do mv and create a link. Then, try access that  inside fakechroot.

If we are referring to fakechroot not being able to handle pre-existing absolute symlinks inside the jail, when we quote from LIMITATIONS, then I think we are talking about the same issue!

Exaclty. I doubt fakechroot could support pre-existing symlinks which points outside the jail because symlinks are resolved by kernel and not by libc.

I wrote example script which relocates symlinks to new root directory:

root=/tmp/testtree; find "$root" -xdev -type l | while read linkname; do target=`readlink "$linkname"`; case "$target" in /*) ln -vsf "$root$target" "$linkname";; esac; done

This script will be included to fakechroot distribution as one of example scripts.
symlinkrelocate.sh script was added to fakechroot distributon. Manual page describes limits of symlink usage.

For others that are reading this, I found out that nodejs uses libuv, which in turns usually uses glibc wrappers for syscalls. However, a recent change from last year made it start using `statx`, a relatively new syscall. Fakechroot works by shimming glibc calls using `LD_PRELOAD` so it can't shim the syscall libuv is calling directly.

So if you want to run nodejs in fakechroot you have three options:
1. If nodejs is dynamically linked to libuv (via `--shared-libuv` build flag), then you can patch libuv.
2. If nodejs is statically linked to libuv (the much more common one), then you have to patch libuv in the nodejs repository, and build node yourself. I built one for node `v12.6.2` and I pushed the binary to DockerHub `openllb/node:fakechroot` for my usage.
3. The proper way is to contribute to libuv. Glibc 2.28 already had `statx` support, so we just need to update libuv to that, and then bump libuv in nodejs.

This only occurs with glibc 2.33 and this PR, when using `fakeroot fakechroot chroot /some/dir some-command` as opposed to `fakechroot chroot /some/dir fakeroot some-command`.
Sadly, this means it's the more common and easier to use variation of the two that breaks.

Stepping through the call, I see the following trace

```
#0  0x00007ffff7f995e0 in stat64 () from [...]/lib/libfakeroot.so
#1  0x00007ffff7fb8d73 in stat64 () from [...]/lib/fakechroot/libfakechroot.so
```

and after one step this becomes

```
#0  0x00007ffff7fa8f70 in __xstat64 () from [...]/lib/fakechroot/libfakechroot.so
#1  0x00007ffff7fb8d73 in stat64 () from [...]/lib/fakechroot/libfakechroot.so
```

which shows the problem, because both of these functions expand the chroot path, which must only happen once.
Note that glibc implements `stat64` by calling `__xstat64`. Removing one is not an option because both need to be intercepted, but it seems that it would suffice for libfakechroot to implement its `stat64` by calling its own `__xstat64` directly. There are a couple of prerequisites you need for this to work:

 * have native *and* foreign architecture libfakechroot and libfakeroot installed on the outside
 * have qemu-user installed
 * set up `FAKECHROOT_CMD_SUBST` with at least:
      * chroot => /usr/sbin/chroot.fakechroot
      * mkfifo => /bin/true
      * ldconfig => /usr/libexec/mmdebstrap/ldconfig.fakechroot
      * ldd => /usr/bin/ldd.fakechroot
      * ischroot => /bin/true
 * set up `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` with all the directories you find referenced by `/etc/ld.so.conf` inside the chroot
 * add /usr/lib/$deb_host_multiarch/fakechroot as well as /usr/lib/$deb_host_multiarch/libfakeroot to your `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`
 * set `QEMU_LD_PREFIX` to your chroot directory

All of this is done by `mmdebstrap` to allow for foreign architecture fakechroot support. If you do not want to use mmdebstrap, read its code and just replicate what it does which includes what I listed above.
